title: B. Geometric Constructions — Detailed Reference
description: Geometric vocabulary for the multi-sheeted n-gon tiling project, covering polygons, polyhedra, tilings, adjacency structures, and specific constructions such as pinwheels, Penrose, and Kelvin structures.

polygon.summary: A two-dimensional polytope: a closed planar figure bounded by straight line segments.
polygon.definition: A **two-dimensional polytope**: a closed planar figure bounded by straight line segments. Polygons are the basic tiles of 2D tilings.

polyhedron.summary: A three-dimensional polytope: a solid bounded by flat polygonal faces meeting at straight edges.
polyhedron.definition: A **three-dimensional polytope**: a solid bounded by flat polygonal faces meeting at straight edges. Polyhedra are the basic 3D tiles.

polytope.summary: The n-dimensional generalization of polygons and polyhedra: a region of ℝⁿ bounded by flat (n−1)-dimensional facets.
polytope.definition: The **$n$-dimensional generalization** of polygons and polyhedra: a region of $\mathbb{R}^n$ bounded by flat $(n{-}1)$-dimensional facets.

vertex.summary: A corner point of a polygon or polyhedron — a 0-dimensional face.
vertex.definition: A **corner point** of a polygon or polyhedron — a 0-dimensional face.

pentagon.summary: A five-sided polygon whose angular deficit forces a multi-sheeted cover in the reconnection framework.
pentagon.definition:
A **five-sided polygon**. The regular pentagon has an interior angle of $108°$, an angular deficit of $360° - 3 \times 108° = 36°$ when three pentagons meet at a vertex, symmetry group dihedral $D_5$ of order 10, and lies in the field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$.

The pentagon's failure to tile the plane (deficit $\neq 0$) is precisely what forces a **multi-sheeted cover** in the reconnection framework.

examples.title: Angular deficit at a vertex
examples.body: When three regular pentagons meet at a vertex, the angles sum to $3 \times 108° = 324°$, leaving a deficit of $360° - 324° = 36°$. This nonzero deficit prevents flat periodic tiling.

examples.title: Multi-sheeted cover
examples.body: The $36°$ deficit forces a 10-sheeted cover (rotations by multiples of $36°$) to absorb the angular shortfall across sheets.

formulas.description: Interior angle of a regular pentagon.
Angular deficit when three pentagons meet at a vertex.

interior-angle.summary: The angle inside a polygon at one of its vertices.
interior-angle.definition:
The angle inside a polygon at one of its vertices. For a regular $n$-gon:

$$\theta_n = \frac{(n-2)\pi}{n}$$

formulas.description: Interior angle of a regular n-gon.

variables.n: number of sides of the regular polygon

angular-deficit.summary: The shortfall between a full rotation and the sum of interior angles meeting at a vertex; a nonzero value prevents flat periodic tiling.
angular-deficit.definition:
The shortfall

$$\delta = 2\pi - \sum_k \theta_k$$

between a full rotation and the sum of interior angles meeting at a vertex of a candidate tiling. Pentagon: $\delta = 36°$ when 3 pentagons meet. A nonzero deficit prevents flat periodic tiling; it can be absorbed by curving the surface, adding extra pentagons (5+), or **transitioning between sheets** in a multi-sheeted cover.

examples.title: Pentagon vertex
examples.body: Three pentagons meeting at a vertex: $\delta = 360° - 3 \times 108° = 36°$. This forces a multi-sheeted cover.

formulas.description: Angular deficit at a vertex of a candidate tiling.

variables.\\theta_k: interior angle of the k-th polygon meeting at the vertex

platonic-solids.summary: The five convex regular polyhedra: tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.
platonic-solids.definition:
The five **convex regular polyhedra**:

| Solid        | Faces        | Field                  |
| ------------ | ------------ | ---------------------- |
| Tetrahedron  | 4 triangles  | $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$ |
| Cube         | 6 squares    | $\mathbb{Q}$           |
| Octahedron   | 8 triangles  | $\mathbb{Q}$           |
| Dodecahedron | 12 pentagons | $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$ |
| Icosahedron  | 20 triangles | $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$ |

tetrahedron.summary: A Platonic solid with 4 triangular faces, 4 vertices, and 6 edges; self-dual.
tetrahedron.definition: 4 triangular faces, 4 vertices, 6 edges. Self-dual. Smallest Platonic solid. Field: $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$.

octahedron.summary: A Platonic solid with 8 triangular faces, 6 vertices, and 12 edges; dual to the cube.
octahedron.definition: 8 triangular faces, 6 vertices, 12 edges. Dual to the cube. Field: $\mathbb{Q}$.

dodecahedron.summary: A Platonic solid with 12 pentagonal faces; the 3D analogue of the pentagon, inheriting all pentagonal-tiling obstructions.
dodecahedron.definition: **12 pentagonal faces**, 20 vertices, 30 edges. Field: $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$. Dual to the icosahedron. The dodecahedron is the **3D analogue** of the pentagon, inheriting all of its pentagonal-tiling obstructions.

examples.title: Dihedral angle
examples.body: The dihedral angle of a regular dodecahedron is approximately $116.57°$, which determines how copies wrap around shared edges.

icosahedron.summary: A Platonic solid with 20 triangular faces; source of 3D quasicrystals and icosahedral symmetry.
icosahedron.definition: **20 triangular faces**, 12 vertices, 30 edges. Field: $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$. Dual to the dodecahedron. Source of 3D quasicrystals (Shechtman's AlMn alloy, AKN tilings).

examples.title: Dihedral angle
examples.body: The dihedral angle of a regular icosahedron is approximately $138.19°$.

examples.title: Quasicrystal connection
examples.body: The icosahedral symmetry group underlies the AKN tiling and Shechtman's 1984 discovery of quasicrystals in AlMn alloys.

rhombic-dodecahedron.summary: A polyhedron with 12 rhombic faces; the Voronoi cell of the FCC lattice that tiles space periodically.
rhombic-dodecahedron.definition: A polyhedron with **12 rhombic faces**. Voronoi cell of the FCC lattice. Tiles space periodically.

truncated-octahedron.summary: The only Archimedean solid that tiles space periodically by itself; forms the Kelvin honeycomb.
truncated-octahedron.definition: The **only Archimedean solid that tiles space periodically by itself**. Result of truncating each vertex of an octahedron. Its honeycomb is the **Kelvin structure**.

examples.title: Face composition
examples.body: Each truncated octahedron has 14 faces: 6 squares and 8 hexagons.

triacontahedron.summary: A 30-faced polyhedron with golden rhombic faces; serves as the acceptance window for 3D icosahedral quasicrystals.
triacontahedron.definition: A **30-faced polyhedron** dual to the icosidodecahedron. Its rhombic faces are golden rhombi. Serves as the **acceptance window** for 3D icosahedral quasicrystals in the cut-and-project method.

dihedral-angle.summary: The angle between two faces of a polyhedron meeting at a shared edge.
dihedral-angle.definition: The **angle between two faces** of a polyhedron meeting at a shared edge. For a regular dodecahedron: $\approx 116.57°$; for an icosahedron: $\approx 138.19°$. Dihedral angles determine whether copies of a polyhedron can wrap consistently around an edge.

examples.title: Dodecahedron
examples.body: Dihedral angle $\approx 116.57°$.

examples.title: Icosahedron
examples.body: Dihedral angle $\approx 138.19°$.

duality.summary: A correspondence between polyhedra exchanging vertices and faces while preserving combinatorial structure.
duality.definition:
A correspondence between polyhedra **exchanging vertices and faces**:

- Cube ↔ octahedron
- Dodecahedron ↔ icosahedron
- Tetrahedron ↔ tetrahedron (self-dual)

Duality preserves combinatorial structure while swapping dimensions.

examples.title: Dodecahedron–Icosahedron duality
examples.body: The dodecahedron has 12 faces and 20 vertices; the icosahedron has 20 faces and 12 vertices. They are dual to each other.

tiling.summary: A covering of a space by tiles with no gaps and no overlaps (except on lower-dimensional boundaries).
tiling.definition: A **covering of a space by tiles** with no gaps and no overlaps (except on lower-dimensional boundaries). In $\mathbb{R}^2$, tiles are typically polygons; in $\mathbb{R}^3$, polyhedra.

honeycomb.summary: A space-filling tiling of ℝ³ by polyhedra.
honeycomb.definition:
A **space-filling tiling of $\mathbb{R}^3$**. Examples:

- Cubic honeycomb (cubes).
- Kelvin honeycomb (truncated octahedra).
- Tetrahedral-octahedral honeycomb (mix of tetrahedra and octahedra).

examples.title: Cubic honeycomb
examples.body: The simplest honeycomb: all of ℝ³ filled by unit cubes aligned to the integer lattice.

monohedral-tiling.summary: A tiling using only one tile shape (up to congruence).
monohedral-tiling.definition: A tiling using **only one tile shape** (up to congruence). The pinwheel tiling is monohedral (one right-triangle shape with leg ratio 1:2).

examples.title: Pinwheel tiling
examples.body: The Conway–Radin pinwheel tiling is monohedral: every tile is a right triangle with legs in ratio 1:2, though tiles appear in infinitely many orientations.

kelvin-structure.summary: The space-filling tiling by truncated octahedra, conjectured by Kelvin to minimize surface area among equal-volume partitions.
kelvin-structure.definition: The space-filling tiling by **truncated octahedra**. Each tile has 14 faces (6 squares, 8 hexagons). Conjectured by Lord Kelvin (1887) to minimize surface area among equal-volume partitions — later disproved by the Weaire–Phelan structure.

tetrahedral-octahedral-honeycomb.summary: Space-filling tiling combining tetrahedra and octahedra in ratio 2:1, built on the FCC lattice.
tetrahedral-octahedral-honeycomb.definition: Space-filling tiling combining **tetrahedra and octahedra in ratio 2:1**. Built on the FCC lattice. Both tile types appear.

penrose-tiling.summary: The famous aperiodic tiling of the plane with 5-fold symmetry, using two prototiles; a cut-and-project image of ℤ⁵.
penrose-tiling.definition: The famous **aperiodic tiling of the plane** with **5-fold symmetry**, using two prototiles (kites and darts, or thick and thin rhombi). Cut-and-project image of $\mathbb{Z}^5$. Both a tiling and a quasicrystal.

pinwheel-tiling.summary: An aperiodic tiling of ℝ² by right triangles with leg ratio 1:2, exhibiting infinitely many tile orientations.
pinwheel-tiling.definition: An aperiodic tiling of $\mathbb{R}^2$ by **right triangles with leg ratio 1:2**. Famous for exhibiting **infinitely many tile orientations** — the triangle copies rotate by all multiples of $\arctan(1/2)$, which is irrational.

examples.title: Irrational rotation
examples.body: Because $\arctan(1/2)$ is an irrational multiple of $\pi$, the set of orientations $\{k \cdot \arctan(1/2) \mid k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ is dense in $[0, 2\pi)$.

quasicrystal.summary: An aperiodic structure with long-range order and crystallographically forbidden symmetries, most famously 5-fold.
quasicrystal.definition: An **aperiodic structure** with long-range order and forbidden (crystallographically impossible) symmetries — most famously 5-fold. Discovered by Shechtman (1984) in metallic alloys.

examples.title: Shechtman's AlMn alloy
examples.body: In 1984, Dan Shechtman observed icosahedral diffraction patterns in an AlMn alloy, demonstrating 5-fold symmetry incompatible with classical crystallography.

akn-tiling.summary: The 3D analogue of Penrose tiling: an aperiodic tiling of ℝ³ with icosahedral symmetry built from two golden rhombohedra.
akn-tiling.definition: The **3D analogue of Penrose tiling**: an aperiodic tiling of $\mathbb{R}^3$ with **icosahedral symmetry**, built from two prototiles (acute and obtuse golden rhombohedra).

cut-and-project.summary: A general construction of quasicrystals by projecting selected points of a higher-dimensional lattice onto a physical subspace.
cut-and-project.definition:
A general construction of quasicrystals:

1. Take a higher-dimensional lattice $L \subset \mathbb{R}^N$.
2. Decompose $\mathbb{R}^N = E_\parallel \oplus E_\perp$ (physical + perpendicular).
3. Select lattice points whose projection to $E_\perp$ lies in a bounded window $W$.
4. Project these selected points to $E_\parallel$.

The result is a Delone set with quasiperiodic order.

examples.title: Penrose tiling
examples.body: Penrose tiling is the cut-and-project image of $\mathbb{Z}^5$ with a pentagonal acceptance window in the perpendicular 2D subspace.

examples.title: AKN tiling
examples.body: The AKN tiling uses a 6D ambient lattice with a triacontahedral acceptance window.

acceptance-window.summary: The bounded region W ⊂ E⊥ filtering ambient lattice points in the cut-and-project construction.
acceptance-window.definition: The **bounded region $W \subset E_\perp$** filtering ambient lattice points. Window shape determines tiling combinatorics. For Penrose: pentagonal window in 5D ambient lattice. For AKN: triacontahedral window in 6D.

adjacency-graph.summary: A graph encoding tile adjacency, with vertices as tiles and edges between tiles sharing an active edge/face generator.
adjacency-graph.definition:
A graph encoding tile adjacency:

- **Vertices**: tiles of the tiling.
- **Edges**: between tiles sharing an **active edge/face** generator.

This graph carries the combinatorial geometry used in spectral, diffusion, and dimension analyses.

centroid.summary: The geometric center of a polygon or polyhedron; often used to label tiles in algorithms.
centroid.definition: The **geometric center** of a polygon or polyhedron. Often used to label tiles in algorithms.

edge-midpoint.summary: The midpoint of an edge; center of edge half-turns in 3D pinwheel constructions.
edge-midpoint.definition: The **midpoint of an edge**. Center of **edge half-turns** in 3D pinwheel constructions.

generator.summary: A group element (reflection, half-turn, or rotation) used to build up the expansion family by repeated application to a seed tile.
generator.definition: A group element (typically a reflection, half-turn, or rotation) used to **build up the expansion family** by repeated application to a seed tile.

active-edge.summary: An edge (2D) or face (3D) carrying a generator operation; crossing it maps one tile to its neighbor.
active-edge.definition: An edge (2D) or face (3D) **carrying a generator operation**. Crossing an active edge maps one tile to its neighbor.

inactive-edge.summary: An edge or face carrying no generator (mere decoration) or a weak gauge generator (sheet transition without spatial translation).
inactive-edge.definition: An edge or face **carrying no generator** (mere decoration) or a weak gauge generator (sheet transition without spatial translation).

active-set.summary: The subset of edges/faces used as generators in a pinwheel construction.
active-set.definition: The **subset of edges/faces used as generators** in a pinwheel construction.

edge-restricted-reconnective.summary: A polygon that fails full reconnection but reconnects when its generator set is restricted to a subset of edges.
edge-restricted-reconnective.definition: A polygon that **fails full reconnection** but reconnects when its generator set is **restricted to a subset of edges**. The pentagon is an example: not all five edges can act as generators simultaneously without forcing tree growth.

examples.title: Pentagon
examples.body: The pentagon cannot use all five edges as generators simultaneously without forcing tree growth, but reconnects with a restricted active set.

reflection.summary: An isometry fixing a hyperplane and reversing orientation, with determinant −1.
reflection.definition: An **isometry fixing a hyperplane** (a line in 2D, plane in 3D) and reversing orientation. Determinant $-1$.

face-reflection.summary: A reflection across a face plane of a polyhedron; an improper isometry used as a 3D generator.
face-reflection.definition: A **reflection across a face plane** of a polyhedron. Improper isometry. Used as a 3D generator.

half-turn.summary: A rotation by π (180°): about a point in 2D or about an axis in 3D.
half-turn.definition: A **rotation by $\pi$** (180°). In 2D about a point; in 3D about an axis.

edge-half-turn.summary: A rotation by π about an edge axis of a polyhedron; the 3D analogue of a 2D half-turn used in pinwheel constructions.
edge-half-turn.definition: A **rotation by $\pi$ about an edge axis** of a polyhedron. Proper isometry of determinant $+1$. The 3D analogue of a 2D half-turn used in pinwheel constructions.

orientation.summary: An element of the rotation group attached to a tile, recording its current angular state.
orientation.definition: An element of the **rotation group** attached to a tile, recording its current angular state. Two congruent tiles can occupy different orientations in the tiling.

orientation-group.summary: The subgroup of O(n) generated by rotational parts of all generators; finiteness is a key reconnection criterion.
orientation-group.definition: The **subgroup of $O(n)$** generated by rotational parts of all generators. **Finite orientation group** is one of the reconnection criteria (Criterion 1): infinite orientation group forces the expansion family to be a tree.

affine-map.summary: A map x ↦ Ax + b combining a linear transformation A and a translation b; the basic building block for tile-to-tile transformations.
affine-map.definition: A map $x \mapsto Ax + b$ combining a **linear transformation** $A$ and a **translation** $b$. The basic building block for tile-to-tile transformations.

formulas.description: General form of an affine map.

affine-group.summary: The group of all affine maps of ℝⁿ, decomposing as a semidirect product ℝⁿ ⋊ GL(n).
affine-group.definition: The **group of all affine maps** of $\mathbb{R}^n$, with composition. Decomposes as a semidirect product $\mathbb{R}^n \rtimes GL(n)$.

formulas.description: Semidirect product decomposition of the affine group.

lattice.summary: A discrete subgroup of ℝⁿ generated by n linearly independent translations; equivalently, the ℤ-span of a basis.
lattice.definition: A **discrete subgroup of $\mathbb{R}^n$** generated by $n$ linearly independent translations. Equivalently, $\mathbb{Z}$-spans of a basis.

examples.title: FCC lattice
examples.body: The face-centered cubic (FCC) lattice underlies the tetrahedral-octahedral honeycomb and has the rhombic dodecahedron as its Voronoi cell.

voronoi-cell.summary: The region of space closest to a given lattice point; Voronoi cells of a lattice tile ℝⁿ monohedrally.
voronoi-cell.definition: The **region of space closest to a given lattice point**. Voronoi cells of a lattice tile $\mathbb{R}^n$ monohedrally. The Voronoi cell of FCC is the rhombic dodecahedron.

examples.title: FCC Voronoi cell
examples.body: The Voronoi cell of the FCC lattice is the rhombic dodecahedron, which tiles space periodically.

branched-cover.summary: A covering with ramification points where multiple sheets meet; the pentagon's multi-sheeted cover branches at vertices.
branched-cover.definition: A covering with **ramification points** where multiple sheets meet. The pentagon's **multi-sheeted cover** branches at vertices: each vertex is a branch point where the angular deficit accumulates.

sheet.summary: A copy of ℝⁿ in a multi-sheeted covering space, indexed by an element of the fiber group.
sheet.definition: A **copy of $\mathbb{R}^n$** in a multi-sheeted covering space, **indexed by an element of the fiber group**. Tiles live on specific sheets.

sheet-index.summary: The label s ∈ G identifying which sheet a tile lives on; different sheets carry the same tile shape with different rotational states.
sheet-index.definition: The **label $s \in G$** identifying which sheet a tile lives on. Different sheets carry the same tile shape but with different rotational states.

sheet-transition.summary: A map between sheets associated with crossing an edge/face; an element of the fiber group encoding how angular deficit is absorbed.
sheet-transition.definition: A map between sheets associated with **crossing an edge/face**. Element of the **fiber group**. Encodes how the angular deficit is absorbed.

fiber.summary: The preimage of a point under the projection π: ℳ → ℝⁿ in a covering space; for a k-sheeted cover, each fiber has k elements.
fiber.definition: The **preimage of a point** under the projection $\pi: \mathcal{M} \to \mathbb{R}^n$ in a covering space. For a $k$-sheeted cover, the fiber over each non-branch point has $k$ elements.

foliation.summary: A decomposition of a manifold into parallel leaves; sheets in a multi-sheeted cover foliate the total space as a stack of ℝ² copies.
foliation.definition: A decomposition of a manifold into parallel leaves. Sheets in a multi-sheeted cover **foliate the total space** when interpreted as a stack of $\mathbb{R}^2$ copies.

vortex.summary: A topological defect at a vertex around which sheet transitions accumulate; encircling it yields nontrivial holonomy.
vortex.definition: A **topological defect at a vertex** around which **sheet transitions accumulate**. Encircling a vortex once yields a nontrivial holonomy (sheet shift); encircling it the right number of times returns to the original sheet.

reconnection.summary: The property that an expansion family closes into a globally consistent adjacency graph rather than diverging as an infinite tree.
reconnection.definition: The property that an expansion family **closes into a globally consistent adjacency graph** rather than diverging as an infinite tree. The central goal of the framework.

local-finiteness.summary: The property that every compact region contains finitely many tiles; a bare-minimum requirement for a valid tiling.
local-finiteness.definition: Every **compact region contains finitely many tiles**. A bare-minimum requirement for a valid tiling. Failed when the cyclotomic density trap occurs.
